clue.text: Sort of holiday some rugby players must have time for

parts.note: the pack is the eight forwards — only some of a rugby side
an age = a long time

explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' is the fair-play word: a pack is part of a rugby side, never the whole fifteen. The surface, players hoping for a break, keeps both halves sounding like sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A package holiday bundles flights, hotel and transfers into one purchase, so the word names that sort of holiday by the deal it arrives as.

clue.text: Maintains focus for cryptic clues

indicators.note: a focus is the central point of something, so the word it governs yields only the letter at its centre

parts.note: seven letters, and the fourth — the middle one — is P
clues = leads, the things a detective follows up

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is describing what you are looking at, which is the joke, and both halves of the wordplay come out of those same two words rather than from anywhere else in the sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead innocence is to maintain it: both verbs mean asserting something and sticking to it, in court or out of it.

clue.text: Without using tons, strangely it does not enhance crisp flavour

indicators.note: to go without something is to do the job in its absence, so the tons never get into the mixture at all
a thing done strangely comes out other than it went in, and letters are no exception

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for a ton, so 'tons' is two of them — and both are left out
the same words once both Ts have gone: fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends to be sceptical about something that is plainly true of crisps. Bank the abbreviation: one ton is T, so a plural asks for the letter twice.
explanation.definitionFit: It is one of the two or three flavours every crisp aisle carries, so the definition names the answer by example rather than by meaning.

clue.text: David Beckham makes one eat dessert first

indicators.note: 'first' fixes where a piece goes rather than what it is — the pudding is served at the front of the build, not at the end of the meal

parts.note: afters = pudding, the course that comes after the main
to have lunch is to eat it

explanation.walkthrough: Beckham's name has been on a range of men's fragrances for years, so the opening words are the definition and not a joke about football.
explanation.definitionFit: He licenses his name to men's grooming products, so the 'one' he makes is a scent — a definition by the celebrity product rather than by the word.

clue.text: Silver lining — occasionally he'll get two below par

indicators.note: a lining sits inside the thing it lines, so the silver goes within the letters rather than beside them
what happens occasionally happens every now and then instead of all the way through, so only every other letter is taken

parts.note: every second letter of hE'lL gEt
AG is the chemical symbol for silver, from argentum

explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver lining' is an idiom pulled in two: the silver is a chemical symbol and the lining is an instruction, and neither has anything to do with clouds.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf a hole played two strokes under par is an eagle — the bird names the score, one better than a birdie.

clue.text: Cup of tea turned up with a little Bounty Bar?

parts.note: a brew is British slang for a cup of tea

indicators.note: turned means flipped round, so the word up is read backwards
only a little of the word is taken, its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Bounty

explanation.surface: Someone sips a cuppa and nibbles part of a coconut chocolate bar.
explanation.walkthrough: A Bounty is a coconut chocolate bar, which makes 'Bar' look like confectionery; it is a pub. A brewpub brews its own beer on site.
explanation.definitionFit: A brewpub is a pub that brews its own beer, so it is one kind of bar, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Supply gum rubber — wanting metre on new roll?

indicators.note: supply read as supple-y, bendy, so the letters are bent into a new order
wanting means lacking, so the metre's letter is missing from the mix

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A request for elastic, minus a measurement, to go on a fresh roll of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' is read as supple-y, meaning pliant, rather than provide; the letters of GUM RUBBER and N, without M, are bent into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A burger bun is the soft bread roll a hamburger is served in, one kind of roll, hence the question mark.

clue.text: 2 seconds to read advertising watchdog's email

indicators.note: a second is the one after the first, so each word here gives up whatever letter is standing in position two

parts.note: rEad — second letter
aDvertising — second letter
wAtchdog's — second letter
eMail — second letter

explanation.walkthrough: '2 seconds' reads as no time at all and is really two jobs in two words: the number points across at another answer, and the plural picks the letters. The watchdog is a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: The definition is the cross-reference: 2 down is CHEESE, and this is the round red Dutch one, so it belongs to that class.

clue.text: Walkman — perhaps as Spooner relates playing …

indicators.note: play is loose movement — the give in a rope or a rudder — so letters with play in them will not stay where they were put

parts.note: fourteen letters, exactly the fourteen wanted, in another order

explanation.walkthrough: Naming Spooner sends you hunting for swapped opening sounds. Here the reverend is not an instruction at all — his name is raw material, and 'playing' is the only order given.
explanation.definitionFit: Walkman was Sony's brand of the thing, so the definition names the answer by its most famous example, which is what 'perhaps' admits.

clue.text: … one from The Strokes (unoriginal pop group, according to him)

indicators.note: him refers back through the ellipsis to Spooner, so swap the opening sounds of the two words

parts.note: hack work is unoriginal, done to order
a band is a pop group

explanation.surface: A sneer at The Strokes, the New York rock band, as a derivative act.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis ties the clue to the one before, which names Spooner, so 'him' is the reverend. The Strokes looks like the New York band but means tennis strokes.
explanation.definitionFit: A backhand is one of the basic tennis shots, played with the back of the hand facing the ball.

clue.text: Possibility of outlet store finally opening

indicators.note: the last letter of store comes at the opening, in front of the outlet
finally picks out the last letter of the word before it

parts.note: last letter of store
a vent is an outlet for air or gas

explanation.surface: The chance that a factory outlet store will at last open its doors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening' looks like a shop opening but places the letter at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: An event can mean a possible occurrence, as in 'in the event of', so it stands for a possibility.

clue.text: I worked with cash register she's discarded — it's old

indicators.note: dough is worked — pushed about until it takes a different shape, which is what happens to these letters
to discard is to throw away, so those four letters are gone before any shuffling starts

parts.note: the setter's own I, one letter of the mixture
twelve letters with four thrown away
S, H, E and S — the four letters discarded from CASH REGISTER

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a small shop being cleared out. A long anagram with a deletion inside it is best checked by counting: twelve letters, minus four, plus one makes nine.
explanation.definitionFit: Geriatric is the medical adjective for aged, used loosely of anything long past its best, so it stands for the plain word.

clue.text: Confused as senior coppers demanded …

parts.note: a DI is a detective inspector; more than one of them gives DIs
to order something is to demand it

explanation.walkthrough: Police ranks are worth banking — DI for inspector, DS for sergeant, PC for constable — and pluralising an abbreviation with S is standard, which is what hides the join here.
explanation.definitionFit: Something disordered has been thrown out of its order, and a mind in that state is confused — one word covers a messy room and a muddled head.

clue.text: … commanding officer essentially use the truncheon

parts.note: CO is the military abbreviation for commanding officer
the essence of a word is its central letter, so this takes the middle letter of each of use and the

explanation.surface: An officer ordering the use of a truncheon.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to the previous clue but adds nothing to the parse. 'essentially' works on each of the next two short words in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosh is a short heavy club, a British word for a bludgeon or police baton.

clue.text: Allowed to take caravan briefly — that is assuming posh car up front is connected? Not so

indicators.note: the first part is placed up front, before the rest
to assume something is to take it on, so the car goes inside

parts.note: IE is the abbreviation of id est, that is
RR stands for Rolls-Royce, a posh car

indicators.note: the allowed word takes the vehicle inside it

parts.note: allowed means let

indicators.note: briefly means in short form, so the front of caravan is dropped

parts.note: caravan cut down to its everyday short form

explanation.surface: Permission to tow a caravan, assuming a Rolls-Royce leads the way, all hooked up.
explanation.walkthrough: VAN is the short form of caravan; the question 'is connected?' answered 'Not so' defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something irrelevant has no bearing on the matter in hand, so it is not connected to it.

clue.text: Firm steal something many people like to drive

definitions.text: something many people like to drive

parts.note: firm = hard, unyielding
a steal is a bargain — something bought far too cheaply

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' is the giveaway once you stop picturing cars. Both halves are everyday synonyms, which is why the surface glides past without sounding like wordplay at all.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive a hard bargain is to negotiate ruthlessly — the definition works on the whole idiom, not on either word by itself.

clue.text: Can rule Tottenham's first 11 out — ultimately not up for it

indicators.note: the answer to 11 across is DISORDERED, so it tells us to put the letters in disorder

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: first picks out the first letter of the word

parts.note: first letter of Tottenham

indicators.note: ultimately picks out the last letter of the word before it

parts.note: last letter of out

explanation.surface: A football fan doubts the Spurs first eleven can rule, and wants them out.
explanation.walkthrough: '11' looks like the Tottenham team, but it refers to the answer of 11 across, which serves as the anagram signal. Tottenham are a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone reluctant is unwilling, not keen or ready to do something, not up for it.

clue.text: Made cloudy as former students smoked

parts.note: an OB is an old boy, a former pupil; more than one gives OBs
smoking meat or fish is one way of curing it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Smoked' does quiet work: curing covers salting and drying as well, so the clue offers one example of the wider word. OB for old boy is standard crossword shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: To obscure something is to dim or blur it, so glass or a sky that has been made cloudy has been obscured — same tense, same sense.

clue.text: See 2
Goodness — neighbour's entrance buzzer rings with excessive force — I must hide

indicators.note: with means alongside, so the second part follows
the buzzer forms a ring around the letter

parts.note: a bee buzzes, so a buzzer

indicators.note: the entrance of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of neighbour

indicators.note: the letter must hide away, vanishing from the word for force

parts.note: violence is excessive force

explanation.surface: A neighbour leans on the doorbell with far too much force, and someone has to hide.
explanation.walkthrough: The doorbell picture makes 'buzzer' a bell, but it is a bee. Goodness is the definition at the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Benevolence is kindly goodwill towards others, a synonym of goodness.

clue.text: See 7
Teasing related to exploit

parts.note: to play with someone is to tease them, and play is jest — 'said in play'
on = about: a book on birds is a book related to birds

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, each of which could be the definition, which is what makes the split hard to find. ON for 'about' is a workhorse — two letters out of a preposition.
explanation.definitionFit: To play on someone's fears is to exploit them: the phrasal verb means working a weakness for your own ends.

clue.text: Show off contribution to murder

definitions.meaning: to boast loudly about a win, the way a rooster sounds off at dawn
a murder is the collective noun for these birds, so one of them helps make one up

explanation.walkthrough: 'Murder' is the trap — a crime in the surface, a collective noun in the definition. The bird's is the best known of all of them, which is what makes the joke land.
explanation.definitionFit: Crowing is boasting loudly over a triumph, and a murder is the collective noun for the birds, so a single one is a contribution to it.

clue.text: A Western losing Oscar — that's unexpected

indicators.note: losing means the letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: occidental means western
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A cowboy film fails to win an Academy Award, which was unexpected.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Western' a film and 'Oscar' the award; they are the adjective occidental and the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: Something accidental happens by chance, so it is unexpected or unplanned.

clue.text: One wood is perfect

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
deal is fir or pine timber, sold as sawn planks

explanation.walkthrough: Deal is the piece to learn: it looks like a bargain or a hand of cards, and in crosswords it is very often the softwood instead.
explanation.definitionFit: An ideal solution is a perfect one — the adjective sense, meaning nothing about it could be improved.

clue.text: Perhaps Rosemary is writing her book

parts.note: taken straight from the clue. The same letters also run on unbroken across neighbouring clue words, a coincidence of the pieces sitting side by side; the setter gives no hidden-word signal.
b = book, the standard abbreviation

explanation.walkthrough: Rosemary is a woman in the surface and a plant in the definition, and the capital letter costs the setter nothing — every clue begins with one.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosemary is one of the kitchen herbs, so the definition works by example, and 'Perhaps' is the flag that says as much.

clue.text: It must go through on time they regularly stress

indicators.note: the word must pass through the others, going inside

parts.note: RE means on, concerning, as in a memo heading
an era is a period of time
taken as written

indicators.note: regularly takes every other letter

parts.note: alternate letters of they

explanation.surface: People insist that a job must be pushed through on schedule.
explanation.definitionFit: To reiterate a point is to repeat it for emphasis, to stress it.

clue.text: Order Andrew's source to meet King Charles, say

indicators.note: to meet means to come up against, so the parts join end to end
the source of a word is where it starts, its first letter

parts.note: first letter of Andrew
R is for rex, Latin for king
Ray Charles was an American singer and pianist

explanation.surface: Prince Andrew arranges a meeting with King Charles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King Charles' looks like the monarch, but the king is R and Charles is Ray Charles, the soul singer.
explanation.definitionFit: An array is an ordered arrangement, and to array things is to set them in order.

clue.text: Fool taking smack maybe loves to escape

indicators.note: the loves escape, leaving the rest behind

parts.note: doing drugs is taking them, so taking gives doing
a smack is a small sailing boat used for fishing
love is zero in tennis, an O, so two loves give two Os

explanation.surface: An idiot on heroin, with romance fleeing.
explanation.walkthrough: Smack looks like heroin with 'taking', but it is a fishing boat, and 'taking' itself is the slang word doing.
explanation.definitionFit: A dingbat is informal slang for a stupid or eccentric person, a fool.

clue.text: Drunk dwelt on disappointment

indicators.note: a drunk cannot walk a straight line, and letters in that state will not stay in the order they were given

parts.note: seven letters, the seven the answer needs, in a different order

explanation.walkthrough: Dwelling on something is exactly what people do with a disappointment, which is why the surface holds together — and the fodder sits in plain sight as the sentence's verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A let-down is the flat feeling left when something promised fails to arrive, so it is a plain noun synonym.
